cultivar: Hubei medium-leaf population bushes of the Xianning hills and neighbouring Hunan Linxiang; mature leaves and stems
processing: Post-fermented: 'lao qing cha' raw material is fired, rolled, sun-dried and then piled in large heaps for weeks to months until dark, after which finer 'face' leaf and coarser 'inner' leaf are steamed and pressed together into dense bricks stamped with the maker's mark, and slowly dried.
harvest_season: Summer and autumn pickings of mature leaf and stems, cut rather than plucked; season is secondary to the long piling.
appearance_dry: A dense, smooth, dark olive-brown brick, traditionally about 1.7 kg (smaller sizes exist), with a stamped character on the face and a finer layer of leaf over a coarser core.
appearance_wet: Coarse dark olive-brown leaves and stems, still firm.
taste_profile: Mellow, woody and straw-sweet with a mild earthiness, a clean, slightly dry finish and very little aroma; built for boiling with milk.

brewing.notes: Pry, rinse twice, boiling water, longer steeps for the dense leaf; the classic way is to simmer 8 g per litre for 5 minutes and add milk and a pinch of salt, Mongolian style.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year and factory in 1.7 kg and smaller bricks; market lots run 2–10 years, with 1990s and 2000s bricks from the Zhaoliqiao factory traded as aged tea. It is drinkable the year it is made but kinder after two or three.
description:
Qing Zhuan is the brick tea of the old tea road north. It comes from Yangloudong, a trading town in Chibi in south-east Hubei where merchants pressed bricks for Mongolia and Russia from the eighteenth century on, and the 'Chuan' character stamped on the face – the mark of a long-gone trading house, kept by the state factory at Zhaoliqiao that inherited the trade – is still what Mongolian buyers look for. 'Green brick' refers to the olive tint of the pressed leaf, not to green tea.

The raw material is 'lao qing cha', mature leaf and stems that are fired, rolled, sun-dried and then piled in big heaps for weeks or months, far longer than Anhua or Liu Bao piling, until the leaf is dark and the harshness has gone. The brick is built in layers – finer leaf on the faces, coarser in the middle – steamed, pressed very hard and slowly dried, which is why it is so dense and keeps so well in a saddlebag.

In the cup it is mellow, woody and straw-sweet with a mild earthiness, a clean, slightly dry finish and not much aroma; it gives six or seven steeps after two rinses with boiling water, but it is really a kettle tea, simmered and drunk with milk and salt as it is across Inner Mongolia. The mistake is to brew it delicately and conclude it is dull.

It is sold by pressing year and factory, mostly in the traditional 1.7 kg brick and in smaller gift sizes, and it is one of the cheapest dark teas per gram. Look for a dry, dense brick with a sweet, woody smell and sharp stamping; crumbly or musty bricks were stored badly. Older bricks are traded on the strength of the 'Chuan' mark, and the same factory's red brick (Mi Zhuan, made from black-tea dust) is a different product.

If you already drink Fu Zhuan or Kang Zhuan, Qing Zhuan completes the set of China's three great border bricks, and it is the plainest and most honest of them.
history:
Qing Zhuan belongs to Yangloudong in southern Hubei. In the Qianlong reign, Shanxi merchants set up houses there with names like San Yu Chuan and Ju Sheng Chuan, first making a rounded 'hat' tea and then rectangular bricks.

Russian, German and Japanese traders joined local ones in the Xianfeng and Tongzhi years, and the tea became a staple of the road north. Mongolian salted milk tea is still commonly made from it. After 1949 the town's factories were merged into what became the Zhaoliqiao factory, whose Chuan-character line carries the name on. Zhaoliqiao brick-making is part of the Chinese tea heritage listed by UNESCO in 2022.
